name.text: Finding the mistake in an angle calculation

questiontext.text:
VABC is a pyramid with angle BAC = \(90^\circ\) and VA vertical. AB = {@pp@} cm, AC = {@qq@} cm and VA = {@rr@} cm. Mutua worked out angle BVC. His working has one mistake.

[[jsxgraph width="360px" height="280px"]] (function() { var b = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, {boundingbox: [-1.2, 5.0, 7.2, -1.5], axis: false, grid: false, keepaspectratio: true, showNavigation: false, showCopyright: false, pan: {enabled: false}, zoom: {enabled: false}}); // oblique projection: receding edges at 30 degrees, half length function P(x, y, z) { return [x + 0.5*y*Math.cos(Math.PI/6), z + 0.5*y*Math.sin(Math.PI/6)]; } var solid = {strokeColor: '#000000', strokeWidth: 2, fixed: true, highlight: false}; var hid = {strokeColor: '#000000', strokeWidth: 1.5, dash: 2, fixed: true, highlight: false}; var dot = {strokeColor: '#000000', strokeWidth: 1.5, dash: 1, fixed: true, highlight: false}; var tx = {fixed: true, highlight: false, useMathJax: false, fontSize: 15, anchorX: 'middle', anchorY: 'middle'}; var cx = 2.4, cy = 1.4; function lab(Q, s) { var dx = Q[0]-cx, dy = Q[1]-cy, r = Math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy) || 1; b.create('text', [Q[0]+0.42*dx/r, Q[1]+0.42*dy/r, s], tx); } function seg(Q, R, o) { b.create('segment', [Q, R], o); } function mark(Q, R, S) { // right-angle mark at Q between QR and QS function u(X) { var dx = X[0]-Q[0], dy = X[1]-Q[1], r = Math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy); return [0.3*dx/r, 0.3*dy/r]; } var a = u(R), c = u(S); b.create('polygon', [[Q[0]+a[0], Q[1]+a[1]], [Q[0]+a[0]+c[0], Q[1]+a[1]+c[1]], [Q[0]+c[0], Q[1]+c[1]]], {fixed: true, highlight: false, fillOpacity: 0, vertices: {visible: false}, borders: {strokeColor: '#000000', strokeWidth: 1, fixed: true, highlight: false}}); } // corner pyramid VABC: angle BAC = 90 degrees, VA vertical (shape only) var A = P(0,0,0), B = P(6,0,0), C = P(0,5,0), V = P(0,0,4); seg(A,B,solid); seg(B,C,solid); seg(V,A,solid); seg(V,B,solid); seg(V,C,solid); // AC is hidden behind the face VBC: dashed seg(A,C,hid); mark(A, B, C); mark(A, B, V); mark(A, C, V); lab(A,'A'); lab(B,'B'); lab(C,'C'); lab(V,'V'); })(); [[/jsxgraph]]

The diagram is not drawn to scale.

  • Step 1: \(\mathrm{VB} = \sqrt{{@pp@}^2 + {@rr@}^2} = {@d2(VB)@}\)
  • Step 2: \(\mathrm{VC} = \sqrt{{@qq@}^2 + {@rr@}^2} = {@d2(VC)@}\)
  • Step 3: [[if test="is(er = 3)"]]\(\mathrm{BC} = {@pp@} + {@qq@} = {@BCs@}\)[[else]]\(\mathrm{BC} = \sqrt{{@pp@}^2 + {@qq@}^2} = {@d2(BC)@}\)[[/if]]
  • Step 4: [[if test="is(er = 4)"]]\(\cos \mathrm{BVC} = \frac{\mathrm{VB}^2 + \mathrm{BC}^2 - \mathrm{VC}^2}{2 \times \mathrm{VB} \times \mathrm{BC}} = {@d4(cs)@}\)[[else]]\(\cos \mathrm{BVC} = \frac{\mathrm{VB}^2 + \mathrm{VC}^2 - \mathrm{BC}^2}{2 \times \mathrm{VB} \times \mathrm{VC}} = {@d4(cs)@}\)[[/if]]
  • Step 5: angle BVC = \({@d1(shown)@}^\circ\)

(a) Which step has the mistake?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

(b) Find angle BVC correct to 1 decimal place. Keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer.

[[input:ans2]] \(^\circ\) [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
(a) [[if test="is(er = 3)"]]Step 3 is wrong: triangle ABC has a right angle at A, so BC is found by Pythagoras, not by adding AB and AC.[[/if]][[if test="is(er = 4)"]]Step 4 is wrong: that formula gives the angle at B. For the angle at V, the side opposite V is BC, so \(\mathrm{BC}^2\) is the term subtracted.[[/if]][[if test="is(er = 5)"]]Step 5 is wrong: the calculator was in radians. In degrees the inverse cosine gives about \({@d1(ok)@}^\circ\).[[/if]]

(b) \(\mathrm{VB}^2 = {@s2p@}\), \(\mathrm{VC}^2 = {@s2q@}\), \(\mathrm{BC}^2 = {@s2b@}\). \(\cos \mathrm{BVC} = \frac{{@s2p@} + {@s2q@} - {@s2b@}}{2 \times \sqrt{{@s2p@}} \times \sqrt{{@s2q@}}} = {@d4(csok)@}\), so angle BVC = \({@d1(ok)@}^\circ\).

questionnote.text: ix={@ix@}, er={@er@}, p={@pp@}, q={@qq@}, r={@rr@}, shown {@d1(shown)@}, angle {@d1(ok)@}

questiondescription.text:
Three-Dimensional Geometry: finding the mistake in an angle calculation

Grade 12 CBE Core 2.4: Find the wrong step in a worked cosine-rule calculation of an angle between two edges of a pyramid and give the correct angle.

Core

This question is original to this project.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

feedbackvariables.text: early: is(ans1 = "s1" or ans1 = "s2"); c1: is(ans1 = "s1"); c3: is(ans1 = "s3"); c4: is(ans1 = "s4"); e3: is(er = 3); rdf: is(abs(csr - float(floor(10000*csok+1/2)/10000)) > 1/10^6);

truefeedback.text:
[[if test="c1"]]

Step 1 is right: VA is vertical, so triangle VAB has a right angle at A and \(\mathrm{VB} = \sqrt{{@pp@}^2 + {@rr@}^2} = {@d2(VB)@}\).

[[else]]

Step 2 is right: VA is vertical, so triangle VAC has a right angle at A and \(\mathrm{VC} = \sqrt{{@qq@}^2 + {@rr@}^2} = {@d2(VC)@}\).

[[/if]]

falsefeedback.text:
[[if test="c3"]]

Step 3 is right: triangle ABC has a right angle at A, so Pythagoras gives \(\mathrm{BC} = \sqrt{{@pp@}^2 + {@qq@}^2} = {@d2(BC)@}\).

[[else]][[if test="c4"]][[if test="e3"]]

The formula in step 4 is the right one for the angle at V: BC, the side opposite V, is the one subtracted. Mutua put his own lengths into it correctly and got {@d4(cs)@}. Check where each of those lengths came from.

[[else]]

Step 4 is right: for the angle at V, the side opposite V (BC) is the one subtracted. [[if test="rdf"]]His value {@d4(cs)@} comes from lengths rounded to 2 decimal places; full accuracy gives {@d4(csok)@}. That is a rounding difference, not the mistake.[[else]]His value {@d4(cs)@} is correct.[[/if]]

[[/if]][[else]]

Step 5 follows from step 4: with the calculator in degrees, the inverse cosine of {@d4(cs)@} is \({@d1(shown)@}^\circ\). So step 5 only carries a mistake made earlier. Check the lengths and the formula.

[[/if]][[/if]]

feedbackvariables.text: okr: is(ans2 > 0 and ans2 < 180); rdn: float(ans2*%pi/180); b2v: if okr then float(s2p+s2q-2*sqrt(s2p*s2q)*cos(rdn)) else NA;

truefeedback.text: That is Mutua's answer, which contains the mistake.
That is angle VBC, at B. Angle BVC is opposite BC.
That is angle VCB, at C. Angle BVC is opposite BC.
Your calculator is set to radians. Set it to degrees (DEG) and work out the angle again.
Your answer is close but not accurate to 1 decimal place. Keep full calculator accuracy until the end, then round the angle once.

falsefeedback.text:
[[if test="okr"]]

Steps 1 and 2 are right. With those lengths and your angle at V, the cosine rule gives \(\mathrm{BC}^2 = {@d2(b2v)@}\). Triangle ABC has a right angle at A with AB = {@pp@} cm and AC = {@qq@} cm: work out \(\mathrm{BC}^2\) from it and compare.

[[else]]

An angle of a triangle is between \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\). Check your working and your calculator mode.

[[/if]]
